A set of provisions, first enacted in 1807 and broadened in 1861 and 1871, that lets the President use the armed forces and federalized militia inside the United States to suppress insurrection, enforce federal law, or protect civil rights when ordinary enforcement fails.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 2 Stat. 443](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/2/443){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 10 U.S.C. 251-255](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/251?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- 10 U.S.C. 251: deployment at the request of a state legislature or governor.
- 10 U.S.C. 252: deployment to enforce federal law when unlawful obstruction or rebellion makes ordinary enforcement impracticable.
- 10 U.S.C. 253: deployment to protect constitutional rights that a state cannot or will not protect.
- 10 U.S.C. 254: requires a proclamation ordering insurgents to disperse before forces are used.

## Why it matters

It is the main statutory exception to the [Posse Comitatus Act](posse-comitatus-1878.qmd). A 2006 expansion made through that year's defense authorization was repealed in 2008, and reform proposals since 2020 have focused on defining its triggers and adding time limits and judicial review.

## Current status

In force. The sections were renumbered from 10 U.S.C. 331-335 in 2016.
